titulo: The History of Prime Numbers: From Euclid to AI
descripcion: From Euclid's 2,300-year-old proof to the AI agents that broke RSA factoring records in September 2026: the sieve, Gauss's pattern, twin primes, the 41-million-digit record prime found with GPUs, why primes protect your bank, and when RSA gets retired.
fuentes: Scientific American on Luke Durant's GPU search: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/new-prime-number-41-million-digits-long-breaks-math-records
Polymath, bounded gaps between primes retrospective: https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.8361

escenas.texto: On September third, twenty twenty-six, an engineer posted a single number online. A hundred and thirty digits long. It broke a record that had stood for six and a half years.
That number was one of the two prime factors of RSA two sixty, a code-breaking challenge from nineteen ninety-one. And the software that cracked it was built with an AI agent.

result.label: the year the challenge was set

escenas.texto: Sixteen days later, a researcher at Anthropic used Claude to break the record again. To understand why that matters for your bank account, we need to go back two thousand three hundred years.
Chapter one. The atoms of numbers.
A prime is a whole number bigger than one that can only be divided evenly by one and itself. Two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen.

Every other number is built by multiplying primes together. Twelve is two times two times three. A thousand is two cubed times five cubed. And here's the beautiful part: every number has exactly one recipe.
That's why mathematicians call primes the atoms of arithmetic. And people have been chasing them since ancient Greece.
Chapter two. Euclid's proof.
Around three hundred BC, Euclid asked a simple question. Do the primes ever run out? His answer is one of the most elegant arguments ever written.

visual.sub: his proof still works 2,300 years later

escenas.texto: Imagine you had a complete list of every prime. Multiply them all together, then add one.
That new number leaves a remainder of one when you divide it by any prime on your list. So either it's a brand new prime, or it's made of primes you missed. Either way, your list wasn't complete.

visual.titulo: DIVIDE BY ANY PRIME ON THE LIST → REMAINDER 1

items.texto: Or it's built from primes you missed
So no list can ever be complete

escenas.texto: Try it with the first six primes, and you get thirty thousand and thirty one. It isn't prime. It's fifty nine times five hundred and nine. Two primes that weren't on the list.
So the primes never end. There are infinitely many. But finding them is another story.
Chapter three. The sieve.

About sixty years after Euclid, Eratosthenes found a clever way to catch them. Write out the numbers. Keep two, and cross out every multiple of two. Keep three, and cross out its multiples. Then five. Then seven.
Whatever survives is prime. Twenty five of them under a hundred. Computers still use versions of this trick today.
But look closer and something strange appears. The primes thin out. Among the first hundred numbers there are twenty five. Among the hundred numbers right after ten million, there are only two.
Chapter four. The pattern in the chaos.

visual.sub: Gauss, Riemann and the prime number theorem

escenas.texto: In seventeen ninety two, a fifteen year old named Carl Friedrich Gauss counted primes in blocks of a thousand. He noticed they thin out in a very specific way, following the natural logarithm.

visual.sub: how many primes up to x

escenas.texto: Up to a million, that simple formula predicts about seventy two thousand primes. The real answer is seventy eight thousand, four hundred and ninety eight. And the bigger you go, the closer the ratio gets to one.
Gauss couldn't prove it. Bernhard Riemann made the key breakthrough in eighteen fifty nine, and in eighteen ninety six two mathematicians finally proved it, independently, in the same year.

visual.titulo: FROM A GUESS TO A THEOREM

escenas.texto: Riemann also left behind a question nobody has answered since. It's worth a million dollars, and we made a whole video about it.
Chapter five. Twins.
Some primes come in pairs, just two apart. Three and five. Eleven and thirteen. Forty one and forty three. Does that keep happening forever? Nobody knows.
In twenty thirteen, a little known mathematician named Yitang Zhang proved that there are infinitely many prime pairs less than seventy million apart.

visual.label: the first proven gap
visual.note: infinitely many prime pairs this close

escenas.texto: Seventy million sounds huge, but before Zhang, nobody could prove any limit at all. Within a year, mathematicians working together online, joined by James Maynard, pushed it down to two hundred forty six. The goal is two. It's still unsolved.
Chapter six. Giants.
Today's champion is two to the power of a hundred thirty six million, two hundred seventy nine thousand, eight hundred forty one, minus one. Written out, it has more than forty one million digits.
It was found in October twenty twenty four by Luke Durant, a former Nvidia engineer. He rented thousands of server GPUs, spread across seventeen countries.

visual.cpu_label: ordinary PCs held the record for 28 years

escenas.texto: A GPU in Dublin flagged the number. Another, in Texas, confirmed it was prime. He spent close to two million dollars. The prize was three thousand.
Notice the hardware. The same kind of chips that train artificial intelligence are now the best prime hunters on Earth. Keep that in mind.
Chapter seven. Primes guard your secrets.

In nineteen seventy seven, Rivest, Shamir and Adleman turned primes into a lock. The idea is a trap door. Multiplying two huge primes takes a computer a fraction of a second. Going backwards, from the product to the two primes, is brutally hard.

That one way street became RSA, and for decades it has protected logins, websites, software updates and digital signatures. A standard RSA key today is two thousand forty eight bits. That's a number six hundred seventeen digits long.
Chapter eight. The AI record.

Back in nineteen ninety one, RSA Laboratories published a list of giant numbers and dared people to factor them. For years, the record was a two hundred fifty digit number, cracked in twenty twenty with about two thousand seven hundred years of computer time.

Then, this September, Eric Lu at the company Cognition factored RSA two sixty. His AI agent, Devin, wrote a new version of the factoring software for GPUs and ran it on spare capacity. About fifteen days. About four hundred thousand dollars.

items.texto: AI agent built a GPU factoring engine

escenas.texto: Sixteen days later, Stephen Weis at Anthropic used Claude to port the same open source tools to GPUs. Up to two thousand forty eight of them, in about ten days, cracked an eight hundred ninety six bit number. A new record.

items.texto: Claude ported the software to GPUs
Up to 2,048 GPUs on idle capacity

escenas.texto: So, is your bank account in danger? Not from this. By Cognition's own estimate, a real twenty forty eight bit key is about ninety one billion times harder than RSA two sixty.

The real threat is quantum computers. In nineteen ninety four, Peter Shor showed that a big enough quantum computer could factor these numbers fast. That machine doesn't exist yet. But the world is already moving.

NIST published new quantum resistant standards in twenty twenty four. And in October twenty twenty six, it set the deadline: RSA is deprecated after twenty thirty, and disallowed after twenty thirty five.
Chapter nine. Still a mystery.

Twenty three centuries after Euclid, primes protect the internet, push our biggest computers, and now AI helps us hunt them. And we still can't answer questions a child could ask. Are there infinitely many twin primes? Where exactly is the next prime?
Next time, we'll open up something you use every day: what really happens in the two seconds after you tap your credit card. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
